MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 4
1:1: March 1992 "Return"
1. Gaepo-dong, March 1992
The rules of engagement have changed already.
#
Within a month of their arrival from Australia, Mrs. Helen Koh found her family a
suitable apartment in a good school district in Seoul. The middle-class neighborhood of Gaepo
was not as nice as where her sister Sonya lived but it had to suffice. After paying the key money

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 5
for the annual lease, which consumed the bulk of their savings, and replacing the most urgent
things before their shipping container from Sydney could be delivered, there just wasn’t room in
the budget for anything better.
From the outset of their marriage, Helen’s husband John had put his sensible wife in
charge of the household finances. Her thrift and fine judgement allowed him to focus on his work
as a manager at a trading company. For almost two decades, on Monday mornings, Helen gave
her husband a weekly allowance for his carfare, meals, and pocket money, then it was her job to
make due with the remainder of his salary for their tithes, overhead expenses, and retirement
savings, if any, and in that order. A former math major at Seoul National University, John
preferred problems he could solve on paper, and family life had far too many unknown variables.
Raising three children was costly, and Helen, a former English major at Ewha Womans
University, worked as a retail sales associate to supplement John’s steady income, which was
inadequate for their mounting needs. John’s work had taken the Koh family to Paramus, Seoul,
and Sydney, in each city, Helen’s supervisors recognized her talent as a reliable salesperson.
Every academic year, for each of the three Koh children, Helen kept a spiral notebook,
and on the back flap, she pasted a manila envelope where she tucked away cash for their school
fees, clothing, and sundries. This year’s envelopes were lighter than usual because the children
had needed many new things upon their return to Korea. In addition to school uniforms, the boys
required larger sneakers, thicker winter coats, and stacks of study guides. The girl, the youngest,
had not grown as much as her brothers, so her main wardrobe would serve another year;
however, in Sydney, the child had needed to see specialists, which had wiped out her portion of
the savings.

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 6
Unlike their rental house in Campsie, a suburb of Sydney, which had four bedrooms, a
den, and a generous backyard for cookouts, their Seoul apartment was on the third floor of a
five-year-old building that had been built out quickly by mediocre developers. Their rental unit
had three small bedrooms and a decent sized living room and two baths. The largest bedroom
went to the two boys—Bo and D.H.; Helen and her husband John occupied the medium-sized
bedroom, and the tiny one near the foyer was for Mido, the child Helen worried about the most.
Her daughter Mido was 13 years old and in the first year of the local middle school. The
girl was short and slight for her age and often mistaken for a much younger child. Like her father
John, Mido had small, round eyes, which made an endearing expression when she smiled. Like
him, she had perfect vision and didn’t need to wear eyeglasses, which the eldest child had
required since he was a toddler. With her dark hair parted in the middle, Mido wore her hair in
two thick braids, which suited her pale, unremarkable demeanor.
Although Mido could speak well enough, she seemed almost incapable of doing so at
school, church, and anywhere else outside the home. With her family, she spoke as needed,
mostly to Helen and the boys. Around her father, Mido was visibly at ease, and on Saturday
evenings, after Mido finished her homework and household chores, the two of them watched
music variety programs on television, smiling and laughing in a wordless cocoon.
All the children were born in Paramus, New Jersey, in the early ‘70s when John worked
at a Japanese trading company and reported to Taehun Shin, who was one year his senior at
university. Shin had been like a brother to John throughout school; military service in the elite
KATUSA unit where their English language skills only improved; and at the Japanese and
Korean trading companies, which had allowed both men’s families to live overseas as subsidized
expatriates. Due to John’s work, the Koh family lived in New Jersey for five years, Seoul for

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 7
four, then Sydney for almost six, prior to their return to Seoul the month before the start of the
school term.
Throughout her childhood, Mido’s teachers had asked Helen to come in for her
daughter’s excessively quiet manner. At her preschool in Paramus and kindergarten and the first
two years of primary school in Seoul, Mido did not talk much with the other children and was
left out of friendships. At her primary school in Sydney, the teachers had hinted at learning issues
despite her good marks. The teachers encouraged the child to talk more in class, advocate for
herself, and work better in groups.
Helen saw herself as a modern, educated parent, and she wanted to help her youngest.
She took time off from work and visited learning specialists and doctors in Sydney with her
child, who pronounced Mido normal, more or less. A reputable pediatrician said there was
nothing wrong medically with the girl’s hearing or vocal cords. The child psychologist believed
that Mido’s shyness was cultural and all the moving around may have confused her. Asian
children, the school counselor had observed, were often less talkative.
Mido’s father, a high-functioning introvert who managed the natural resources
department at a multinational trading company, dismissed such simplistic nonsense. Not all
Koreans were quiet. His own family had been filled with loud people. They were all deceased
now, but growing up, John had lived with their high noise level. At the slightest provocation or
encouragement, his mother, father, and elder brother would shout and argue their well-articulated
opinions. To be left alone, John had retreated into his studies, excelling at math and foreign
languages. As an adult, he did not ask for much in life. He enjoyed listening to music and being
in the presence of his wife and three children.

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 8
John wanted to comfort his dear Helen who was clearly troubled that their daughter did
not have friends. Throughout her own childhood, Helen, like her elder sister, was a natural social
leader—engaging, kind, and deliberate about her goals and methods. In college, she had served
as vice president of an English poetry society and secretary of a music appreciation group. John
was proud of his appealing wife who spoke remarkably well in both Korean and English in her
calm speaking voice, which matched her thoughtful demeanor.
The father felt less anxious about his daughter’s prospects. Mido was a seventh grader
who read at a college reading level. The other children did not appreciate her, he reasoned. When
ready, she would speak up, make friends, and find the work she was meant to have. She would
grow out of this social reticence, and Helen, a devout woman, prayed he was right. Perhaps Mido
might be different if her self-assured brothers didn’t crowd her with their larger personalities or if
the Koh family hadn’t moved across the world every few years.
John Koh wanted things to be equal for his sons and daughter but recognized their innate
personality differences. Above all, he wanted to protect his daughter’s peace of mind. All this
poking around and extra attention couldn’t be good for children. After all, if you looked hard
enough, you could always find something wrong. The world was too noisy. It was fine for Mido
to be her own way and seek privacy and solitude.
As to be expected of a child who hardly talked and read excessively, Mido received
admirable grades; however, on her report cards, her teachers commented often: “Mido is a fine
student and a good girl. However, she should have more social relationships.”
Helen was accustomed to her sons’ strong school performance and popularity. Her middle
child, DH, was an exceptional soccer player, and the eldest, Bo, was a standout student and the

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 9
teacher’s perennial favorite. Helen was the sort who needed to fix things, and she wanted to
know what she could do to bolster her youngest’s self-esteem. The child didn’t have to be school
president, the prettiest, or the top student; however, the earnest mother wanted her child to be
included.
Although Helen had not wanted to return to Seoul, preferring to raise the children abroad
to enlarge their opportunities, she was relieved to be back home since a little girl could be quieter
here. Mido’s exceptional shyness seemed almost unremarkable in Korea.
#
The middle school was six blocks from the main shopping street and less than a ten-
minute walk from the Koh’s apartment. The four-story cinderblock building with a slate roof,
whitewashed with a dark blue trim, housed numerous classrooms, a spacious auditorium, two
music rooms, and a new gymnasium. There was a well-maintained field for the three grades of
boys and girls. Mido did not attend the coveted middle school in Gangnam which sent the
greatest number of students to the desirable specialized public high schools in the city, but her
school was far from the worst.
In Mido’s homeroom class, there were forty-six students. Mr. Na, the homeroom teacher
who also taught mathematics, assigned Mido, who was smaller than most of the children and
built like a tender sapling, in the second row.
One row behind her, in the center, was Yun Kim—an attractive child with the dark, large
eyes of a bird that noticed the tiniest of things. An exceptional student, she was also known in the
school for being a brilliant sprinter and solid keyboard player. Each year, her homeroom teachers
selected her as the class leader because her peers listened to her. In the morning, Yun’s mother

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 10
French braided her only child’s shoulder-length raven hair, and although all the girls wore
matching uniforms, Yun stood out by wearing imported sneakers from America.
As class leader, it was one of Yun’s tasks to help Mido, the new student from Australia, to
assimilate. On the first day of school, it was Yun who told Mido where to put her lunchbox,
where and when to change into her sports uniform, and what clubs she could join, as well as
where all the meeting rooms were located. Mido did as instructed, never bothering Yun with any
unnecessary questions, and as usual, she kept to herself. Ever an attentive child, Mido was able
to pick up from observation whatever she needed to know.
To make up for her silence around the other girls, Mido smiled often, her pleasant eyes
curving along her round, pink cheeks. Most adults liked her sweet face, but her classmates would
not have considered her as pretty as Yun, whose symmetrical and charming features were often
commented upon with great admiration. Mido’s lack of distinguishing physical charms did not
bother her; if anything, she was relieved not to be noticed.
On the third day of school, about ten minutes before lunch recess, Mr. Na, called on Bora
Kang to solve a math problem. On the bulletin board by the front door, the teachers posted
weekly exam scores, and more often than not, Bora’s name was at the top of most lists to reflect
her status as the highest scorer.
Bora, a serious girl who wore a different colored headband each day, marched to the
board, solved the problem in her neat hand, wiped the chalk dust from her right hand, and
returned to her seat in the next to last row by the window. She tucked her navy pleated skirt
beneath her bottom before sitting, then brushed down the front of her skirt to cover the tops of
her thighs.

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 11
Mido checked Bora’s answer on the chalkboard against her worksheet. There was an
error. Mido should not have multiplied the numerator. Mido rubbed the worn-down ear of her
blue and white puppy eraser against the pencil markings and started again.
Mr. Na called out, “Koh Mido,” and she looked up from her paper and smiled at her
teacher.
“Number 3,” he said, pointing to the board.
Mido swallowed and approached the chalkboard gingerly, bringing her worksheet with
her. She copied her answer on the board with great care.
“Incorrect,” he said, shaking his head, disappointed at how the child got such an easy one
wrong. Out of consideration for her recent arrival to the country, he had assigned her a relatively
simple problem.
Mido bit the inside of her lip then checked her solution against the way Bora had solved
the previous question. She had made the same computation error as before by multiplying the
numerator. Using quick strokes of the chalkboard eraser, Mido wiped off her wrong answer,
smudging the edge of her blue sweater sleeve, to begin again.
“Who told you that you could do that?”
Startled by Mr. Na’s stern tone, Mido froze, realizing that she wasn’t allowed to redo the
problem.
“How can you learn if you do not recognize, admit, and explain your mistake? It does no
one any good if you do not point out your error. You erased the error, so now no one can learn
from what you did wrong. The erasing is like covering a weakness. It’s lying. It’s cowardice and

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 12
selfish.”
Mr. Na had been a college basketball player, who had become a sports radio announcer in
Daegu after graduation. When he couldn’t support his family working at a local radio station
doing a job he adored, he had labored hard to become a middle school mathematics teacher for
his second career, eventually landing in the capital city with his wife and two children. As a
handsome former athlete, female teachers and administrators admired him, and the male teachers
looked up to him for his discipline and dunking skills.
“Koh Mido,” Mr. Na said in his rich tenor voice. “Did you hear my question? How can
you learn if you do not admit then explain your error?”
Perplexed, Mido glanced at him then lowered her gaze just as quickly, having no idea
what he wanted her to do now. Was she supposed to write back her mistake? Tears filled her
eyes.
Crying never moved Mr. Na. It only made things worse. If girls were to succeed in the
world, he believed, they had to be more stoic. As a father, he was as tough on his daughter as he
was on his son. Life was full of terrible disappointment and cruelty, and he didn’t see the
pedagogical purpose of coddling these middle-class girls, who had no idea how easy they had it
compared to his generation and the ones before him.
The teacher crossed his arms and frowned. He didn’t like her face—the features were too
soft and little, and her head was not yet in proportion to her small body. Mr. Na preferred girls to
be bright like a new coin, visually engaging as the loveliest of flowers and with the vitality of
youth in their movements. No doubt this girl was an unmotivated, overindulged child from a rich
family that had lived overseas. He ascribed her puny size to being a picky eater.

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 13
“Go stand by my desk.”
Mido went to the teacher’s large wooden desk by the windowed door. Across the hall,
uniformed boys and girls lined up in size order against the tile bordered wall for lunch recess.
She wished she could bolt through the classroom door and hide in a bathroom stall until her heart
stopped pounding so fiercely.
“Hold out your hands,” Mr. Na said.
Incomprehension clouded her shining eyes.
“Like this.” Mr. Na held out his large, strong ball player’s hands with his pale, lined
palms facing upward. He gathered his palms together, as if to receive a loaf of bread.
Mido crinkled her brow and imitated him. Her palms were three colors, more white and
pink in the center and bluish around the thumbs and fingers. She had never given much thought
to her body and least of all, her own tiny hands.
From his pencil cup, Mr. Na withdrew his brass ruler, one of the first classroom supplies
he’d bought with his initial paycheck as a teacher.
He raised his right hand and struck her open palms with the heavy ruler.
“One,” he said quietly.
Mido grimaced, stunned by the sharp pain.
The class pitied Mido. She’d had no warning. No one had told her that this was
something that happened. The only way to avoid this shame was by getting the answer right, or if
the teacher had an understanding with your mother. Things could be different if your father was
an important person.

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 14
The class leader Yun felt especially guilty for not having mentioned Mr. Na’s golden
ruler, which left red welts across a child’s soft palms.
Tears flowed down Mido’s cheeks, and she regulated her breath the way Dr. Ryan had
taught her to whenever she was afraid. Everyone was watching her get punished but she had to
keep breathing. The gentle, gray-haired doctor from Sydney had told her that when she felt fear
or worry, Mido had to keep inhaling and exhaling. It will be fine, he’d said. Breathe.
“Two,” Mr. Na said calmly, then raised the metric ruler with flourish and swung down.
“Three.”
The class heard the final smack of the metal hitting skin, and the girl stood in her place
without a murmur. The children knew this was the last time.
Three strikes for the third problem.
Mido wiped her cheeks with the back of her left hand. Only after Mr. Na tilted his chin
toward her desk did she bow to the teacher and return to her seat.
“Students, line up,” Mr. Na said, his voice elegant and reasonable. He dismissed them.
#
Yun retrieved her lunch box and Mido’s from the shelves next to where the textbooks
were stored.
“Follow me,” Yun said to the new girl.
When Mr. Na was out of sight, Yun pulled Mido into the washroom.
“I hate him,” Yun whispered. “A real son of a bitch.” Her eyes widened, savoring the

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 15
forbidden salt of the insult. She smiled at Mido, revealing her matching dimples.
Mido blinked back tears. She had gotten the problem wrong, so she was at fault. But no
one had ever hit her before. Not at home or school.
Yun opened the water faucet in the sink.
“You’ll feel better after you wash your face. Go ahead,” Yun said, and Mido obeyed.
From her pocket, Yun retrieved a clean white handkerchief.
“Dry your face. You can’t pay attention to the asshole.”
Mido had never heard any girl talking like this. Even her brothers didn’t use these words.
At her school in Sydney, you could be sent to the principal’s office. Yun was the class leader, and
in their homeroom, she was an ideal and well-spoken student. In the washroom, she was
someone else. Even her pretty face seemed less placid, her teeth clenched, her jaw firm, and in
her anger, the cords of her thin neck became more visible.
Yun examined Mido’s hands. There were pink stripes across the meat of her palms.
“My mother says it’s my fault when the teacher hits me. My father says it’s good for me
to get the shit kicked out of me by the teacher when I’m young because then I’ll study harder.
Grown ups actually think this. Most of the teachers here are pretty nice and never do this, but I’d
heard about Mr. Na from the older students that this could happen. I’m sorry I didn’t tell you.”
Mido couldn’t imagine her parents thinking that this hitting was necessary.
Yun stared hard at Mido’s face, trying to read any meaning behind her dark eyes. Since
school started, the new girl had not spoken beyond the faintest of murmurs of assent for roll call.
It was strange but Mido’s silence had not troubled Yun. In a way, she felt drawn to the new

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 16
student, making Yun feel more useful, which she liked. Sensing that Mido might need a
translator or an advocate, Yun continued talking because it was clear that Mido was paying
careful attention, perhaps more so than anyone else.
“But I disagree with them,” Yun added. “I don’t study harder because the teachers hit me.
I don’t usually get hit but I don’t want to watch anyone else get in trouble either. I just hate the
teachers who do this. There must be other ways to make your point.” The class leader shrugged.
“Anyway, save yourself some trouble at home, and don’t tell your parents what happened today.”
Yun glanced in the metal mirror then looked away as quickly as if the pretty girl in the
reflection was a surprise to her.
“Just imagine if you had messed up Problem 10,” Yun said giggling, and raised both her
hands, splaying all ten fingers. “Ten smacks.”
Mido smiled at the girl. Yun’s cocoa-colored eyes were warm and open. The light spray
of freckles on her button nose resembled a tiny constellation of distant stars across a pale sky.
The girls were of a similar height, but Yun was built like a runner, slight, tan, and
muscular. She also had excellent posture, embodying an admirable self-possession for such a
young person.
“Mido, are you bad at math? I don’t want you to feel worse but that problem wasn’t the
toughest one of the group today.”
Mido shook her head no. In Sydney, she’d received perfect grades in mathematics.
Though here, the math was far more advanced, forcing her to read and re-read the textbook.
Homework took more time. Her brothers, too, had complained about it the night before. Bedtime

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 17
kept getting pushed back because of the difficulty of the school assignments.
“Maybe you have to change your hagwon,” Yun said.
Mido didn’t understand.
“Mr. Na doesn’t know anything. He won’t teach you, but he expects you to get the right
answers. If you get something wrong, he’ll hit you again and again. I heard that when he gets
really fired up, he can use the broomstick on your legs. The ruler’s not so bad, I guess. Two years
ago, I heard he hit a boy so hard that he bled on the back of his calves. Even his mom came in to
complain. Not that it did any good.”
With an imaginary broom handle, Yun’s wiry arms made dramatic swinging motions
below Mido’s knees. She shivered, realizing then that the joke was more scary than funny, and
she looked down at her clean white sneakers.
In the back corner of the classroom where the cleaning supplies were stored, there were
two wooden hand-held brooms, matching dustpans, a basket of rags, and a red plastic water basin
to clean the floors. Everyone hated sweeping, and the only worse rotating duty was waxing the
floors, done on your hands and knees, inhaling the noxious smell of the wax. Mido couldn’t
imagine getting hit with the thick wooden broom handle.
Yun picked up their lunch boxes from the washroom table by the long communal sink.
“When’s your birthday?” Yun turned to Mido. “Mine’s October 9. I’m short, and
everyone thinks I’m the youngest, but I’m not. You’re not tall either. Are you older than me?”
Mido shrugged.
“When? When is your birthday?” Suddenly, Yun felt entitled to an answer.

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 18
At last, Mido replied, “October 1.”
Yun tapped Mido’s shoulder with her bony fist.
“Yaah! You do talk. I knew you did.”
Mido looked confused, unable to comprehend why everyone cared so much about
speaking all the time.
“Eight days difference is nothing. We’re almost twins. We could have been in the hospital
at the same time.” Yun grasped Mido’s left hand.
“Let’s go eat. My mother put sausages and dumplings in my lunchbox today, and I have a
box of Peppero. I’ll give you some. You know what? You should go to Eagle Academy with me.
For English, I have Sean Teacher. I study Math with Henry Teacher. They’re from America.
Henry Teacher went to M.I.T. That’s a better school than Harvard for math and science. I’ll get
my mother to call your mother. My parents want me to go to college in America so I go to this
special hagwon run by Americans. I mean, they’re Korean but not really. They’re gyopo.” Yun
paused. “I guess like you. Anyway.”
Mido followed Yun keeping a respectful distance, taking care not to step on the girl’s
shadow. The class leader walked with purpose down the wide, yellow linoleum covered hallway,
flanked by rows of classrooms. During recess, Yun chatted to the quiet girl who nodded and
smiled. Her friend had everything figured out for them, and Mido felt grateful to be in her care.

1:2: 1992 "Envelopes"

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 20
2.
#
No one had expected Mido’s teacher to make a home visit.
Beyond the five gray metal folding chairs and laminate conference tables, one serving as
the children’s desk and the other as the dining table, the living room lacked rugs, paintings, or
books. It took no time at all to sweep the bare floors each morning. For the time being, the
children slept in sleeping bags, and Helen and John on borrowed bedding. Except for clothing
and toiletries, Helen’s older sister Sonya had loaned them everything as she had done years
before. There was no reason to buy expensive mattresses or pots and pans when their own
household things would arrive in two months. It was like camping, Helen told her family, and the
children had not complained.
Helen was filling out the application papers for a part-time sales position, which Sonya
had told her about. If she could get this job at the Lotte Hotel duty-free store, Helen would be
able to get home in time to fix dinner and help the children with their homework. Over the years,
she had accumulated sufficient retail experience in Paramus and Sydney, and could provide good
references. Helen didn’t care much for luxury handbags or expensive face creams; however,
having sold enough things in so many places to all different kinds of customers, she had learned
to appreciate better made goods and understood the value of an expensive and rare gift. Here in
Seoul, as a Korean citizen with good English language skills, she could work at the nicest places.
She was only forty-two years old and enjoyed working in sales. If she could get thirty or
forty hours a week with commissions, she would be able to send the children to a nice hagwon
and save.

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 21
When the building security guard buzzed to announce Mr. Na’s arrival, Helen put away
her job application forms into a blue pocket folder.
The teacher bowed as he entered the apartment and removed his black leather shoes. Re-
soled again, not too long ago, Mr. Na had brush polished and buffed his penny loafers to a high
sheen. He prided himself on his neat appearance.
He was a few years younger than Helen and several inches taller than her husband John.
No visible gray hairs. Mr. Na’s clear complexion was tanned from morning runs. He was
noticeably nice-looking with a trim, athletic appearance and white teeth, evidencing his distaste
for cigarettes and coffee. Mr. Na wore a white gold wedding ring and an affordable Japanese
watch.
There was no sofa, so Mr. Na sat down on one of the three folding chairs on the
children’s table and placed his briefcase on the empty chair between him and Helen. He was
disappointed by the drab building and the room without proper furnishings. He’d hoped that
Mido’s family had more means. No servant had opened the door or offered tea. A
commemorative coffee mug from a large downtown church with cold milky coffee rested by a
blue folder.
The teacher looked smart in his gray woolen sweater vest over a crisp white shirt and
necktie with dark slacks, and the mother was in her house clothes, a white cotton tee shirt and a
pair of boys’ navy jogging pants. Doing chores, Helen often wore her sons’ hand-me-downs
since the boys grew so quickly. They sat opposite each other on the smaller conference table.
“Thank you for seeing me today. I wanted to stop by and say hello. I was told that you
had just arrived from Australia. I understand that your daughter was never educated here.”

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 22
“Well, Mido went to kindergarten and her first two grades in Seoul, but my husband’s
work took us overseas again. I’ve tried to keep up the children’s Korean through books and
cassette tapes. Mido is the youngest. She has two older brothers at the high school across town.”
The teacher knew the school. He had been turned down for a job there.
Helen continued.
“In Sydney, the children went to a Korean language school at the church on Saturdays but
I’m not sure how much they learned. I was working,” her voice trailed off, not knowing what he
thought of mothers like her. Nervous, she was talking too much.
Having lived abroad, there were times she didn’t know what to say when she returned
home. Things were constantly changing, especially language and schooling, and often, even
strangers had a word or two to say about her parenting. Natives would correct her when she
made a mistake or didn’t know how a thing had changed and smile like they won something, as
if to say, you might have lived somewhere else but you’re not so special, and Helen didn’t know
how to make them feel better for feeling left behind and disadvantaged by those who had gone
elsewhere when in reality, she felt lost herself.
“This is a nice apartment,” he said. “How many bedrooms do you have?”
“Three. It isn’t very big,” she replied. Their rented house in Sydney had been far more
spacious. “We are still waiting for our furniture.” The apartment felt even shabbier in his
presence, she thought.
“May I get you something to drink? We have coffee.”
“I don’t drink coffee.”

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 23
Helen tried to remember if there was any tea in the nearly empty pantry.
“I live about two hours from here,” he said. “I take the train almost four hours a day
round-trip for my job. It must be wonderful to live so close to the school.”
Helen looked down, embarrassed by what she’d said. He must have thought she was
boasting, and it occurred to her that in a way, she had. A teacher had never visited her home
before.
“Let me get you something to drink. I have some delicious biscuits from Australia.”
Helen went to the kitchen and found cold barley tea in the refrigerator.
The open kitchen faced out to the living room, and in his sight, Helen put together a tray:
two glasses of barley tea and sweets she’d been saving for her husband. She laid out the offerings

Eagle Academy was not a bad place to work. The teachers were well compensated and paid on
time, and the children were motivated. With only ten students per class, everyone was able to
practice writing, listening, and speaking, as well as solving difficult math and science problems.
The parents who paid dearly for after-school and weekend lessons witnessed notable progress—
not a guaranteed outcome for a hagwon even in Gangnam. Eagle Academy’s reputation had
spread, traveling to even Apgujeong, where Helen’s sister Sonya lived.
With long waiting lists, there was almost never any room for new students who were not
siblings of graduates. Sonya’s two boys were already enrolled at the best tutoring center near the

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 56

anything for now. If there were any issues, however, Sonya would have barreled through any

Helen, to push her way into this famed hagwon, only blocks from their house.
Tom Song, the American owner of the tutoring center Eagle Academy, had put up the
sheetrock himself. He and his Korean wife, Clara, had painted each wall and ceiling of the two-
floor space, which they had rented from Tom’s former classmate Renee Cha from Cornell, where
he got his bachelors’s degree in Political Science before getting his doctorate at Teachers
College.
Tom and Clara had divided the two hundred square meter space into six classrooms, one
common area, and two professional offices. Inspirational posters featuring famous inventors,
presidents, and writers lined the corridors. Everywhere you looked, Tesla, Edison, one of the
three Roosevelts—Theodore, Franklin, or Eleanor, and the likes of Shakespeare, Locke, or
Montaigne and their most celebrated quotations encouraged beleaguered minds to persist and
excel.
Though the owner of the hagwon was not a religious man, his wife Clara was, and she
had tacked up Bible verses which few could argue about love and forgiveness, and of course, the
well-known verses from St. Paul exhorting the runner to run his race swiftly. Tom thought the
verses might be good for the students, and indeed, Eagle Academy had flourished. In five years,
Eagle had become the most sought-after hagwon in the area without any advertising. Their
students outperformed their peers but more importantly, they wanted to study there.
Clara, who believed in the power of prayer, spent every evening praying for each of the

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 57
Eagle students by name and concern. The childless couple almost lived at the hagwon, and in the

each student and pray for them and their families,

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 74

For Mido and Yun, third year of middle school was a major improvement, because they had a

John arranged for Danbi Jung to meet him at the glass walled conference room by the bank of

John believed he was a reasonably honest man. Over the course of his life, he had
witnessed many unfair things, which had troubled him. When necessary, he had turned a blind
eye. When he had a duty to report, he had done so but not always. In school, you weren’t
supposed to snitch. In the military, you protected your fellow soldiers. In the office, you took

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 123

ambition and many ill-gotten gains. He loved his wife and children, so protecting them became
his primary constant. All else seemed to be a variable.
He had only worked at trading firms, so by practice, he understood the middleman. Over
the years, clients had offered him money to get a discount from the company. Suppliers had
offered him kickbacks to be selected for a lucrative deal. John never accepted money he didn’t

refusal grew stronger. By this time, the ones in the business knew better than to approach him for
preferential treatment through the wrong means and went to his colleagues or superiors instead.
John Koh’s squeaky cleanness may have been one of the many reasons why he was sent
abroad and kept there even as a young man. Controlling greed protected a company from
catastrophe. Employees who took a packet of cash and turned the other way while favored
suppliers or clients did shoddy business created dangerous situations for the manufacturer,
distributor, and consumer. Both John and his boss Shin believed that financial greed was a
market inefficiency.
Shin’s vices were only women, and he admired that John had a professional conscience

In reality, for John, the big sins had been easy enough to avoid. As men in trading, Shin

John could hardly recall if he had been to this part of Myeongdong. He wasn’t able to recognize
much of it though he’d once had a part-time job around here in college. The record shop, where

1:12 January 1995 "Cho Sisters"

Even as an infant, Helen and John’s first-born had a calm temperament and responsible
disposition, as if he appreciated what it meant to be a jangnam with its attendant privileges and
responsibilities of primogeniture. Bo never seemed to let the burdens of being the eldest child
overwhelm him. He exerted himself in the classroom and on the sports field, he got along well
with his peers. A nice looking and thoughtful young man, Bo was a blessing and a relief to his
busy parents.
Often, Helen’s friends asked: How did she raise her son? Was there a method to rearing
such a fine student and good boy? The credit, however, belonged neither to Helen nor John. Bo

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 150
came that way, she would say.
Bo’s mother could admit this truth not because Helen was modest, but rather, the
experience of having more than one child in the same household amply demonstrated to any self-
aware parent that each child was entirely unique. Eventually, every small human—even flesh of
one’s flesh, which should have provided some illusion of predictability—asserted his
individuality, no matter how much a parent tried to control, shape, or design his formation.
As educated and earnest, middle-class parents, Helen and John had provided more than
the basics, and certainly more than they had been given as children of poor parents. Parenting
was, like it or not, a haphazard experiment for even the best intentioned humans, and Helen and
John observed Bo, DH, and Mido with profound fascination as only parents can with their own
babies. Each child was immutably distinct from the others.
Whenever Helen read or heard about a sad story in the news about a child who had gone
astray, rarely did she assign blame to the parents or their relationship. In a way, life had taught
her that the debate between nature and nurture was almost moot: Excellent parents sometimes
had badly behaved children, and careless parents could have admirably performing progeny. The
bond between a human and her child was binding, yet it had to be loosened. A mother had to
love, and a child had to grow up. The results were often out of one’s hands.
All three children of the Koh family were born in New Jersey, and Bo’s birth and delivery
had been manageable, bearing little relationship with the horror stories of childbirth she’d heard
over the years. Helen recorded the details of his birth in the notebook she kept for Bo:
February 7, 1976. 6:42 P.M. Eight pounds and eleven ounces. Twenty three inches long.
Bo had been neither early nor late, and the labor was a breezy six hours. Even the doctor

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 151
who delivered him was grateful. The charming Dr. Ellison had been able to shower and return
home to his large colonial house in Ridgewood before dinner was on the table.
In America, Bo was almost eighteen years old, but his Korean age was nineteen. He was
tall for a wrestler and built more like a powerful sprinter. Like DH, he could play soccer well
enough, but never enjoyed the running required. Girls admired his glossy chestnut-colored hair,
olive complexion, and large light brown eyes. He spoke English like a native, making him an
exotic curiosity at a public high school in Gangnam, and he studied from morning till night,
almost not needing to sleep. Most remarkably, Bo had maintained an impressive grade point
average in the second stanine nationally, allowing him to apply to Yonsei University. The school
did not think he could test for Seoul National, his father’s alma mater, which was fine by him.
There was a girl he liked, who adored him. Once, she showed up at his hagwon and
invited him to her house to study, and right there in her bedroom, she proposed sex. Stunned,
grateful, and naturally tempted, Bo was still able to control himself and demurred. He made a
deal with her. After they were accepted into college, they would make love. Whenever he
masturbated, he fantasized about the twin possibility of the college of his dreams and the
tantalizing promise of a very pretty girl he cared for wanting to sleep with him.
When Bo failed to be admitted to Yonsei University, he broke up with her. The girl, a
precocious beauty, who was in his homeroom class, had been accepted to Sunkyungkwan
University. The only daughter of two preoccupied college professors told Bo that she would be
happy to wait for him as he prepared to take the Yonsei exam again. Almost everyone took these
exams more than once, especially for schools as hard as Yonsei, she’d said, trying her best to
encourage him. Bo, guilt-ridden at the heavy expense of his failure, told the young woman firmly
that he would not hold her back. To make the situation even clearer, he told her that they should

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 152
not even be friends.
Bo took the national college exam in November 1994, which was called the “1995
Suneung.” In addition, Bo had to take the bongosa, a specific admissions exam for Yonsei
University, and although the bongosa devastated many students, Bo had thought that, for him, the
Yonsei-specific exam had gone well enough.
The bongosa question he could never forget was: “Describe the difference between
digital and analog.”
For his answer, Bo wrote that a digital clock stated a moment in time whereas, an analog
clock revealed the process of time.
Not long after he took the Yonsei bongosa, he and his hagwon classmates rushed back to
their Yonsei exam hagwon, which was different than Eagle Academy, his hagwon for his high
school studies. The bongosa hagwon tutor had been more or less flying blind because there were
almost no prior tests from which to teach. Each student, fresh from having taken the exam, was
asked to recall the test questions, and three tutors recorded the questions and typed out their
speculated answers. Bo’s tutor said his digital versus analog answer was terrific. Not that it
mattered.
Bo’s suneung score was what had kept him out. With 200 being the perfect score for the
“1995 Suneung,” he received 153, a strong score but not invulnerable, and predictably with his
focus on studying for the college exams, his high school grade point average had fallen on the
lower end of the second stanine, so he was no longer in the top 4% nationally.
Bo wanted to take the exams again. Helen did not know what to do.

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 153

Bo took the “1997 Suneung” on Wednesday, November 13, 1996. It was his third try.
He would never forget every detail about the day before the test. On the Tuesday before

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 176
the suneung, Seoul was cloudy and cold. By the middle of the day, it got warmer, about 48
degrees Fahrenheit, and Bo jotted it down on his pocket-sized diary.
After his last hagwon class ended, he took a mostly empty bus to the Yonsei campus and
sat in a window seat near the back and tried to warm himself by tucking the blue woolen scarf
into his faded black parka.
“If you want to be a Yonsei student, you have to behave like one,” Kim Teacher, his
hagwon instructor had told him. “Go to the cafés where Yonsei students have their snacks, read
the books they read, and inhabit the peace of mind of being an admitted student. Visualize. Draw
the picture in your mind.”
Kim Teacher had graduated from Seoul National University—the same school as Bo’s
father—having studied Law. A suneung wizard and a legend for having gotten one of the top
scores of the country for his year, he charged an extraordinary fee to be a suneung tutor, which
Bo’s Aunt Sonya paid. As a bachelor, not yet forty years old, Kim Teacher earned more than
several lawyers and judges combined and already owned two commercial buildings in Hongdae.
It was rumored that he didn’t have to work anymore for money, and it was clear that he enjoyed
teaching. His speciality was re-takers, the ones who had not passed on their first or second tries.
Kim Teacher was convinced that Bo would pass this time. His scores were in the safety
zone, so he focused on preparing Bo’s mental game. He advised Bo to go to the campus at least
once a week to be in the mind of a Yonsei student. After the last class ended, Bo heeded his
teacher’s advice and went to the popular two-story cafe near Sinchon station, frequented by
Yonsei and Ewha students.
At a corner table near the window, Bo picked up a discarded copy of a Yonsei literary

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 177
magazine and read it while having his tea. All around him, young men and women huddled
together, warming their cold hands on hot coffee cups. Attractive girls in bold patterned sweaters
and denim trousers discussed politics in hushed tones, ignoring the boys sniffing around them.
Bo tried to imagine himself being one of the young men writing in their notebooks or
doing their assigned reading. A younger woman who had short permanent waved hair, resembled
Isul, his friend studying for the civil service exam at the motel. She was reading The Stranger in
French. Bo could not remember the last time he’d read a novel. During summers in high school,
he used to read classic European and American novels in English.
He’d always imagined working and living in Korea but he also wanted to be the kind of
Korean who knew more about the world—in books, film, and history.
In less than twenty four hours, he would take the suneung again, and since last
November, he had done little except for study for this exam. He felt good about it and ready to
put it behind him.
After Bo finished his coffee, he walked along the main part of the campus, decorated with

lecture halls, relieved that a period had ended. It couldn’t have been that all the students were
pleased, but everyone appeared calmer than how he felt inside.
Kim Teacher had assured him that this time would be his last. Bo’s practice scores had

Mido was not exactly qualified for the Sydney University Dramatic Society. Nevertheless, she
had a laudable goal for joining SUDS. She wanted to learn how to speak well.
Her boyfriend Tek was a third year at the University of Sydney, and a Director of the
Debating Society. In his second year, he had won the Australian Nationals. An exceptionally
gifted debater, Tek neither missed nor forgot a single word of an opponent. No question or
argument on any topic could ever be put to him, which he could not manage extemporaneously
with elegant logic and persuasive conviction.

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 199
As a general matter, Mido did not wish to opine, complain or quarrel in most social
interactions. She preferred to listen and think. If needed, she’d say something and use words.
Mido was never impolite.
The couple got along well. Tek admired her thoughtful demeanor and restraint. He knew
she wanted to learn how to speak better, and he mentioned her joining the Debating Society. Out
of curiosity and with a good dose of will power, Mido attended the newcomers meeting and said
even less than usual. They agreed that nothing was more unnatural to her than debate.
As a first year university student, Mido had no problems with the written coursework. As
in high school, she found writing research papers and exams enjoyable. She had selected the
Education course, specifically at the Primary level, rather than Secondary, because Mido felt
comfortable being with small children.
After classes, meetings and work, the two undergraduates met at Tek’s rental apartment,
which he shared with old friends from high school.
One Friday afternoon, they made love in the empty rental; fixed scrambled eggs, baked
beans and toast in the common kitchen; then returned to Tek’s room to do their school work.
Mido was seated upright on the bed to do her reading, using two pillows as her lap desk.
Tek was at his desk, which was pushed up against the long wall. Before starting his assignment,
he remembered.
“How did your presentation go?”
Mido inhaled. Everyone had to give a brief talk about their research papers in her primary
school survey course, and it had been abysmal. It was a quarter of her grade.

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 200
“That good?”
She looked at him, her expression full of worry, and sighed.
“When I talk to my tutoring students, even in a group of four or five, I feel fine. I explain
the concepts, ask them questions, and teach what’s needed. I must be doing okay because the
kids are doing well, and I get referrals since their marks improve a lot.”
Mido collapsed bodily into her open book, burying her head in the comforter.
Tek tried his best to understand her point of view. He had debated since year 9, but even
before that, he had been able to handle anyone who interrupted, shouted down, or fought a point
to death in any situation. At his boys’ school, arguing had been a kind of sport, and in a way, he
had been a kind of varsity athlete of talking. Nothing thrilled him more than persuading his
position against another thoughtful opponent. If the opponent was an ass, Tek enjoyed taking him
down even more. He loathed bullshitters—anyone who just liked arguing or talking to get
attention. The better he got at debate, the more he became aware of the responsibilities of the
gifts of logic, rhetoric and argument.
As a skilled debater, he felt more strongly than most that speaking and listening should be
meaningful. If he had to expound on the matter, he would say that the highest point of debate
was to reveal truth and knowledge among well-intentioned people. A mark of a great debater was
to be truthful in the structure of an argument. An assertion based on verifiable evidence, clean
logic, and fair execution of delivery should triumph over a weaker point.
One of things Tek admired about his girlfriend Mido was how she spoke: her words were
essential. There was nothing unnecessary in her thoughts. Whatever she said felt true and
valuable. It upset Tek, having been around so many loudmouths, to think that Mido’s ideas could

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 201
be lost or diminished because she didn’t know how to deliver her thoughts out loud well enough
to others. She spoke fine with him and her family.
His parents, both professors at the University of New South Wales Sydney, had taught
their only son that almost any subject could be learned competently by a student of average
ability, and Tek believed that his girlfriend was beyond average, rather, she was, to him, an
exceptional thinker.
Tek’s parents, who had graduated from Korea University and received doctorates at the
University of Sydney where they had met and married, believed fervently that a child should
never be forced to study. That said, they had provided a number of opportunities for Tek to try

political scientist who specialized in East Asia, and his mother was a well-regarded economist.
Both prided themselves on never pushing a child to excel. Rather, they taught Tek about the need
for intelligent schedules, delayed gratification, and the value of consistent, high-quality work.
Tek’s father argued that Koreans back home had the wrong ideas about education.
“All that memorization, rule-following, and class-ranking. Foolish business,” Professor
Do would mutter.
His wife, Professor Yoon, who went by her family name, would add, “Such willful

It’s not that they idealized the Australian education system; however, they thought it was

The Cellar Theater was showing its age. The black paint needed attention, the curtains

Established in 1865, Josiah Crawford’s Emporium had its beginnings as a dry goods
store, selling cotton fabrics, silks, velvets, ribbons, millinery, gloves, then later, cosmetics,
perfumes, and imported pottery and ceramic ware to a prospering middle class in Sydney. After
the second war, in fits and starts then gradually, the store expanded from a 2,000 square foot shop
to 50,000 square feet of retail space in the most fashionable part of the Harbour City, carrying the
finest collections of brand name merchandise in Australia. Its handbag and leather goods
department rivaled the toniest boutiques of London, New York, and Paris, and the Emporium was

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 214
the exclusive purveyor of the latest luxury imported goods from Europe. In the mid 1970s, the
Crawford family sold the legacy brand to Winchester Hall, an upstart gourmet food purveyor in
the mid 1970s, which put in a stunning food court in the basement level and ran the retail
business with effective corporate fiscal controls.
Starting from the late eighties, Crawford’s best customers were not native Australians but
the most stylish Japanese and Korean tourists who loved the curated selections of the store’s
famed retail buyers.
Helen had worked at Crawford’s for three years until 1992, then moved to Seoul with her
family, then returned a couple of years later. As a senior sales associate, Helen covered high-end
Korean speaking customers. Her manager Scott Cudahy was delighted to have her back.
Scott, a third-generation Aussie, who lived with his wife Olive, was fond of Helen. She
was the sort of employee who could be relied on to support her colleagues when they were in a
crisis and was fair about sharing commissions.
In the imported handbags and small leather goods department, Scott managed six
salespeople, three of whom were Asians —two Japanese and Helen, the Korean. In the past
decade, the Asian sales associates brought in the highest sales commissions. Their overseas
customers were decisive and unstinting in their luxury purchases. At the height of the bubble in
Japan, when a businessman had to buy gifts for his wife or girlfriend, or both, he’d hand over an
itemized list and salespeople wrapped up the purchases, denoting the appropriate labels for the
respective recipients.
The recent financial crisis began mid-summer in Thailand then like dominos spread
across Indonesia, South Korea and then Malaysia, Laos, and the Philippines. The countries had

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 215

corporations couldn’t pay their debts. The failure to protect against currency fluctuations and the
ensuing panic, among other factors, caused the terrible modern devastation.
Helen’s husband John had explained it to her like this.
Just imagine: “You’re a Korean worker who gets paid in Korean Won. You ask a friend
who is going to New York to buy a watch for $1,000 USD on your behalf. She agrees to buy it

think you will owe $1,050.
In November 1996, that 1,050 USD watch cost 840,000 in Korean Won.
In November 1997, that 1,050 USD watch cost 1,048,950 in Korean Won.
Now, you have to cough up the difference of over 200,000 won or $188 USD. You
thought your interest was 5% but it turned out to be almost 12%. Imagine running a razor thin
margin business that’s growing rapidly and needs to borrow like crazy to survive, and out of
nowhere the cost of your debt more that doubles. Of course, you’d no idea that the Korean Won
would depreciate at that rate and that the dollar would become that much stronger. Your salary
hasn’t risen at a comparable rate, nor your investments. You can’t pay her back. Simple.
Helen had not borrowed any money, and she hadn’t purchased any imported watches or

Unlike her younger sister Helen who’d married for love, Sonya Cho had refused to give up her
marriage prospects for romance. Since childhood, Sonya had been clear-eyed and mature about
her few assets. She was beautiful, capable and motivated to perform well. At school and work,
she had outperformed everyone.
Negligent parents and a difficult life had taught Sonya that the combination of talents and
persistence could yield occasional rewards even in the midst of terrible struggles. Neither an
optimist nor a pessimist, by living in the present with great concentration on what was most
important, Sonya had become a gifted adapter and a brilliant problem solver.

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 239
For Sonya, her family was everything. And also God. Self-aware, she knew that if she did
not have faith in her God, she might have become a terrible person. She was wise and sober
when most people were not. Because of her Christian ethics, she refrained from taking advantage
of others; however, she was never unaware of her advantages.
Only a few years after she finished Ewha Womans University, her contemporaries
believed Sonya had won at life by becoming the hand-picked bride of the heir of her employer
Chairman Mun, the owner of some of the costliest real estate in Seoul.
Young-gil, Chairman Mun’s chosen nephew, was a hard worker. Not only was he smart
about people and diabolical in business, he loved his uncle like a father. As the boy of a luckless
divorced mother, he had understood early that his savvy uncle was his only ticket out of the
average life of a salaryman—the best that a person like he could’ve achieved without family
wealth and significant connections.
Young-gil did not want a mediocre life. He wanted grandeur, power, and an extraordinary
wealth that would protect him and his family for generations.
Chairman Mun chose Sonya for him, and Young-gil obeyed. He would’ve preferred a girl
from a higher class of people. However, there was an advantage of marrying someone from an
inferior background: Her people could never look down at him.
Sonya’s parents were itinerant gamblers, who left debts, wherever they lived. The mother,
a coarse, illiterate woman who loved to smoke cigarettes and play go-stop, had done odd jobs,
working more frequently than her husband, who died early from cold exposure while drinking.
At age 42, Sonya’s mother collapsed at a market from a coronary, leaving all three in the
care of a neighbor who made living so difficult that the orphans had to figure things out for

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 240
themselves.
The Cho sisters, Sonya and Helen, applied themselves at school, and with the guidance of
a few upright public school teachers and a collection of priests and nuns, who rooted for the
bright children, ended up graduating from the fine women’s college then married. With a letter of
introduction from a priest, Kenny migrated to Australia where he settled and flourished. The Cho
siblings almost never spoke of their parents or their birthplace.
Chairman Mun had watched his nephew Young-gil grow up and recognized his unstinting
ambition and relentless work ethic. What his nephew needed was not a high society beauty who
would waste time and money on things that did not matter, but rather a diligent, sacrificial, and
ethical girl from a pathetic family like his favorite secretary Sonya, who was also an exquisite
beauty.
Her undisciplined parents had given her no money, education, or pedigree, but she had
been born with the face and body that would rival any Miss Korea. Men used to gape at his
secretary, and ever loyal, appropriate, and virtuous, Sonya’s clear and polite refusal to flirt or
acknowledge their romantic and sexual advances had flattered the Chairman.
Tycoons had asked him privately, “Does Secretary Cho have a boyfriend?” and the
Chairman would demur any requests for a introduction. Wealthy men, by nature more persistent
than poor ones, tried anyway. “Miss Cho, would you make some time for me so I can buy you
something delicious?” the bold ones asked as if the woman could not afford to eat, when for a
secretary she was paid handsomely. Always, Sonya declined.
“If anyone bothers you, please let me know,” the Chairman said, and she’d always
handled it without any fuss.

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 241
The nephew, a canny negotiator, understood that marrying the girl that his uncle had
selected would inure to his benefit. Obedience on such an important decision in a man’s life
would demonstrate the requisite filial piety that even most sons would not practice. Moreover,

The remodeled church basement of Gospel Presbyterian was a cavernous room with soaring
ceilings. It was used for coffee hour, church meals, and assemblies. Set in the back of the room,
facing the north side of the highway, was an impressive platform stage with six steps on each
side.
Yun felt happiest on that painted plywood stage. Apart from her classes and helping out at
Shrimp Castle, she lived for Wednesday praise team rehearsals and service on Sundays. Back in
Seoul, she had resented piano practice and disliked her teacher, whose clothes had smelled of
mothballs. However, if she ever ran into him again, she would’ve thanked him, because she had
turned out to be a competent piano player, able to read music on sight and play almost anything
on the Yamaha keyboard.
After Wednesday evening practice, Yun tidied her sheet music and prepared to leave. She
didn’t want to go home, where her mother Nari would be watching her rented drama videos.
If Nari wasn’t in the middle of a drama series, she would be looking at the Korean news
and talking to the television screen.
At first, when Yun’s family moved to Orange County, her father Joonho had been the
angry one. To him, no one in America had any manners, and her mother was disappointed by
how far they had fallen in the world. But after a few years, in their mid-lives, her father and
mother had retreated, accepting the defeat life had handed them, then her father had taken half
their savings, bought a one-way ticket to Brazil and left. He’d asked Yun to understand that this
would save his life, and in a way, she believed him.
Keeping him in that kitchen at Shrimp Castle was killing him, and she imagined him in a
country that seemed as unreal to her as the moon.

“It depends,” John said.
For once, Nari felt hopeful, believing that Mrs. Chung would give Helen a job and with
John’s help, she could pay off the promissory note on Shrimp Castle on time. She knew her
husband had expected her to lose the business and join him in Sao Paolo, and Nari wanted to
surprise him.
Things had been so difficult, and suddenly, a path had been cleared.

The strip mall in Garden Grove was an enormous rectangle with businesses all along the four
sides of the rectangle as well within the four square islets set in the middle of the black asphalt
ocean of the parking lot, which opened out to the boulevards along the lengths of the mall. The

Shrimp Castle was one of the seven stores on the southern subdivision of the mall, and it
did brisk business because there were no other shops that sold fried foods. The mall was a kind
of Korean neighborhood filled with people, who would never have crossed paths in their
previous lives back home.
Nari’s store was a fifteen hundred square foot shop separated into a dining area, kitchen,

be moved around to seat thirty two customers.

just hadn’t been enough time.

March 12, 1999

Dear Tek,
#
I’m writing to you from the Exodus staff lounge which is the large room near the library, it’s
about the size of my new classroom, and where we also store everything.
Right now by the door, there are six cases of juice boxes, a dozen tubs of pretzel sticks,

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 314
and several pallets of toilet paper and paper towels which need to be put away.
I’ll get to it right after I finish writing this.
Before you frown, it’s not officially my job to organize the supplies, but I do as much as I
can to save Yun and Lion the trouble. What I like about working here is how everyone pitches in.
Even the parents help out when things break down or we need something special.
There’s an extra long conference table near the back wall and a dozen chairs for teachers
to prepare for classes and grade homework. This is also where I eat two meals a day. On the
shorter wall, there’s a refrigerator, coffee machines, two microwaves, and an industrial size sink
and a dishwasher. A rattan laundry basket on the counter is filled with granola bars, cup noodles,
and crisps.
When the door’s closed, the room feels like my sanctuary. I finished preparing for my
class early today, so I thought I’d write. My letters have been infrequent. Forgive me.
For lunch, I’m eating a chicken salad sandwich that I brought from home with a bag of
crisps from here. Every time I have a sandwich, I think of you layering yours with pickle slices
or jalapeño peppers. It would make me laugh when you’d take a bite, and bits of pickle or
peppers fell out of the sides, making a mess. You’d smile like you were pleased. I don’t know if
you do this in front of anyone else, or if you just did it to make me laugh. I never got a chance to
ask you. I hope you’re having good lunches.
Last month was my one year anniversary at Exodus, and Lion gave me a nice raise. Also,
he’s letting me teach one of the boot camp classes for specialized high school admissions tests,
which will start tomorrow. I’ll make an extra $1,500 per session, and if that goes okay, I might
get to do a couple of those per semester. Bo taught those already, and he said I’ll be just fine.

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 315
My new afternoon class is going well. I have twenty-seven students. The work isn’t
difficult.
I was worried because last year, my students were so young, which turned out to be more
babysitting than anything, so I thought middle school kids would be tough, but they’re not that
different from my kindergartners.
My middle schoolers are a little more serious, and they do listen to me, which is a relief.
They’re like nutty puppies. It’s hard to get upset with them because they’re adorable but I do
have to pay attention to all the relationships. The girls have built their own worlds upon worlds,
and the boys are still daft and goofy, which make them a little easier.
Bo is taking two classes at Fullerton College but he’s still driving the hagwon van and
tutoring a few high school kids.
When I have my middle schoolers, I can still see my former little ones who are now in
the first and second grade when they come in. There’s a plexiglass partition separating my room
from theirs.
I feel proud of them. Isn’t that strange?
It’s as if I’m the only one who taught them to put away their things in their cubbies, wash
their hands, and wait quietly for their snacks before worksheets and story time. It’s odd how
much I want to check in on them.
During breaks, they knock on the plexiglass and wave at me. My middle schoolers are
sweet, too, but they’re awkward and funny around each other like little adults. I remember being
self-conscious around that age. How did we ever survive all this, I wonder.

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 316
Sometimes, I go with Bo to take a kid home when his parents can’t make pick up, and I
make sure he gets inside to his apartment while Bo stays in the van. Often, there’s no one home.
Even though my mother always worked somewhere, she was usually home at 2:30pm. Also, I
had my brothers.
I imagine the parents must be concerned but I guess they have no choice. When the kids
whose parents can’t pick them up live in my apartment complex, I just let them stay in our place

“Initially, Maslow argued that human beings had five stages of needs: at the base level
are physiological needs — air, water, food, shelter; then above that is the need for feelings of
safety — the wish to be free from violence but also insecurity. For example, even the need for
insurance because that feels like protection from harm to one’s body or property. Above
physiological and safety needs, is our need for love and belonging. Human beings are social
creatures, and we crave love and community.
“Above physiological, safety, and love needs, we have our need for esteem — both self
esteem and esteem from others. For example, if you are a football player and achieve a
touchdown, you may feel good about yourself, and the crowds may respect your achievement.
The touchdown can do both things.

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 366
“Finally, the top of the pyramid is self-actualization, when a human being fulfills his
potential. Maslow later revised the five and added more over the years, but today, we’ll focus on
the original paper.”
The class wrote down the five.
“The four bottom levels of the pyramid, physiological, safety, love, and esteem are called
‘Deficiency Needs,’ because when we feel deprived of them, we need them even more. Say, if
you are freezing cold, your need for warmth only increases. You are motivated to find a sweater,
a bowl of soup, or better heaters.”
The class nodded and wrote down Dr. Wilson’s examples.
“The fifth stage of self-actualization is called a ‘Being Need,’ because it’s a need to be a
fully developed person. After one’s basic needs are being met, and of course, there are
fluctuations and a wish to maintain these levels, a person will wish to seek her fullest expression
of who she is.”
“In the paper, how does Maslow define ‘self-actualization’?’ ” she asked.

“Even if all these needs are satisfied, we may still often (if not always) expect that a new

“Maslow argued that a human being could wish to seek her maximum potential.

Ten days after the funeral, Tek arrived in California. Work had prevented him from attending
Helen’s services. He’d sent an enormous wreath of white chrysanthemums. He called her more
often and when he missed her, left brief messages on the answering machine. Mido got an email
account, and he sent her messages from his.
Right after work, Mido went to his hotel, and as soon as she walked into his room and
closed the door, she collapsed in to his arms. It was as if they had forgotten their disagreements
and his disappointment for her refusal.
“I’m so sorry, Mido. This was the soonest I could get away.”
Tek’s dark hair was longer in the front than usual. A while back, he’d mentioned
changing his barber. Mido was surprised by how unfamiliar a person could look just from a new
haircut. His fine features—the thoughtful sloping eyes and straight nose, became more distinct,
shaded by his dark hair. He’d lost some weight and his cheekbones were more defined. Tek was
more handsome than before.

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 589
“Are you hungry?”
She wasn’t. The thought of food made her think of her mother, who always asked about
her meals. Mido sat down.
“You must be tired from the flight.”
“No. I’m okay. I was reading this fascinating brief. No kidding. I’m studying it actually.”
Tek picked up the papers beside him and smiled. “Are you tired?”
They were being polite. The last time they were in a room at this hotel, right away, they’d
made love as if two people in love needed to do something to remember each other. Now, it felt
strange to think of sex. Mido didn’t want that.
“How’s work?”
“Fine,” he said. He’d already been called to the NSW Bar and was at Chambers,
supporting the barrister Stephen Jackson. Swamped, Peter had no business being here, but
everyone at Chambers had understood.
Tek had met Helen only a few times, but he had felt her kindness. She was not a frivolous
person. His mother, Professor Yoon, the famous economist, was a college professor, who had
never been interested in being like other mothers; however, from an early age, Professor Yoon
had drilled it into him that women did paid and unpaid work in the house, but it was all work.
When Tek worked for or with women, he’d gotten along well, unlike some of his peers.
What he had learned was that women were often more protective of junior men than junior
women.
“You’re back at the hagwon so soon.”

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 590
“It’s better to keep busy.”
“I felt badly that I couldn’t be here for you.”
Mido understood. In order for this to continue, neither could expect much from the other.
This was how they had managed to last.
Tek had no intention of moving to California. It made no sense, and of course, she
respected it. There was a stronger argument for her to move to Sydney, finish her degree, and to
marry him. However, Mido would not leave her family now. Her income was more important
than ever.
Hospital bills, mortgage for the new house, insurance, taxes, and car payments—all of it
required Mido to help out. They no longer had Helen’s earnings. Bo had two more years of
school, and he said he was interested in becoming a psychologist, which would require a
doctorate, and that could add another six to eight years. DH would graduate law school in two,

“I know.”
“Come back with me. I’m a working barrister. In record time. My offer stands. I can send

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 591
“This can’t go on with you being here and me in Sydney.”
Mido hugged her knees. His reasoning made sense, and she was so tired.
“You’re going to sacrifice your life for your father and brothers? No, Mido. This isn’t

“No, I mean us. I’m not going back.”

4:1 January 2003 "The Rose Salon"
