John had never worked with so many women before.
In his two years as the business manager of the popular Rose Salon, he could name only
two regular male customers, Oliver Bonoba and Nathaniel Rosario, who scheduled monthly
paraffin pedicures. The pedicurists preferred Mr. Bonoba and Mr. Rosario because they tipped
well and never tried any funny business. Unlike other nail salons, there were no massage
therapists, and John had observed that most men were less inclined to pay money for personal

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 595
grooming. Although several technicians had offered, John had never had a manicure or pedicure.
For most of his professional life, he’d worked with men and a few junior women.
Although Taehun Shin had preferred including attractive female office workers for drinks after
work, John had avoided socializing with them one-on-one or in a group.
As the father of a daughter, John hoped that no one would treat his daughter unfairly. A
man, he knew, could get the wrong idea when a woman was just being polite or kind. His
widowed mother had gone through a lot with landlords, bank officers, and shopkeepers, and John
took pains to be as clear as possible, even at the risk of being viewed at rude or cold.
For the past two years, Nari had suggested a salon Christmas party—a tradition from
Mrs. Kwon’s era—but, John had passed on the idea. What most employees wanted was to get
home early and good year-end cash bonuses. When there was a budget line for a party, John split
the money equally among the twenty-four technicians and added it to their year-end bonus
envelopes. Everyone also got a crate of oranges and a tin of butter cookies.
The previous owner, Mrs. Kwon, had called all the workers “girls.” However, after
hundreds of hours of training at Saddlebrook College relating to the nail technician licensing
exam, required for her to legally own the salon, Sonya insisted that all the technicians’ name tags
reflect their preferred status. Everyone was called Miss or Missus, and for the women with
church titles, if they wished, they were addressed as Deacon or Elder.
John preferred the formalities, wanting to keep as much distance between him and the
women. He made sure that he was never alone with anyone anywhere in the shop. The workers
found Manager John Koh, as his name tag read, competent and polite, but far too quiet.
The technicians addressed him as Manager John and the ones who were also members of

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 596
Gospel Presbyterian called him Elder Koh. Many of them were curious about Helen and admired
the widower’s reserve and mourning, believing that he was a man who’d never love another
woman as much as his late wife. When they asked Manager Nari about her, she shared that Helen
was an elegant lady—a graduate of Ewha Woman’s College, a good mother of three fine
children, and a woman of strong faith.
“Was she pretty?” they’d ask, having met Helen’s sister Sonya, the beautiful owner of the
salon, who came by the salon several times a year.
“Oh, yes,” Nari stressed. “She had style, too. Deacon Cho was pretty like her sister but
they looked different. The deacon’s face was softer and more olive-toned, and when she listened
to you, you could tell that she was interpreting you in the best possible way.
To keep from crying, Nari would make a self-deprecating joke.
“She wasn’t tacky. She didn’t wear much makeup or bright clothes. Didn’t talk so much
like me. Almost never watched television.”
For Nari, one of the best things about working at Rose Salon was that she could wear her
clothes from back home, which still fit her—dresses and skirts in jewel-tones and lots of eye
makeup. Her hands were now always perfectly manicured and painted in the latest colors. There
were always women to chat with about the latest drama programs and fashionable clothes in
magazines.
Unlike at Shrimp Castle, where she’d worn a long white apron over her brown and beige
polyester uniform, here, Nari was a manager, and she styled her hair up or down, depending on
the fashion, and she could wear her fanciest things, including any remaining pieces of jewelry
she hadn’t sold when they needed money.

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 597
At the salon, with its mirrored walls and chandeliers, it was appropriate for Nari to wear
sequin skirts and fur trimmed sweaters. For the first time in years, she felt almost attractive
again. After only a week at the salon, she told her daughter, “I feel like a girl.” Not once did she
miss Shrimp Castle, a business that her husband had purchased and left behind.
Several workers had considered pursuing John as a prospective husband, but Nari put
them off. “You can try, but there’s no point,” she’d say. “He’s never going to remarry.” If a
technician or customer tried flirting, perplexed, John would nod politely and return to his tiny
business office, which could barely hold his desk, chair, and filing cabinet.
If he ever needed to talk with a worker in private, he’d schedule the conversation, always
accompanied with Nari, in the employee’s room, which had a mirrored two-way window as well
as security cameras.
Nari believed that none of the women interested in the widower were up to Helen’s
standards. Even if Helen and her sister Sonya came from poor families, Nari had been astonished
by how neither ever seemed intimidated by other educated and wealthy people. Nari didn’t know
if that unwavering personal dignity came from having gone to an elite college or from what
they’d been through and survived. Surely, it wasn’t just money. Nari had once had a great deal of
money, and she hadn’t been astute like Helen, or steely and elegant like Sonya.
Nari had a few regrets. She had graduated from high school with decent marks and had
once considered becoming a nurse, but she’d gotten pregnant with Yun and married. She
believed she would have made a good nurse because she liked helping people. When she and her
husband had plenty of money, Nari had seen no point to studying hard to become a nurse or
learning English properly, which she now sorely regretted. She missed her husband and wished

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 598
she’d been better to him. If Joonho ever returned, she vowed to be more patient.
For five years now, with two businesses, Nari and John had worked together well. Nari
was relieved to sell Shrimp Castle and send money to her husband. Working at the salon was far
easier on her back and knees. Except for the nail dust and chemical smells of the polish and
remover, Nari thought being a sales manager at Rose Nail Salon was the perfect job.
As the business manager, John minded the books, taxes, licensing requirements, lease
management, waste disposal, maintenance, and inventory, and Nari took care of the
appointments and workers.
No different than the customers at Shrimp Castle, often, people mistook them for a
married couple, and Nari would correct them, saying John was her brother-in-law.
She was married, and Joonho would always be her husband. He would return.
If her husband wanted a divorce, he could come back and ask for one. She’d be sad but
give in. Life was too brief to hold grudges, and he had given her many good years and their
beautiful daughter Yun. Nari had no interest in ever getting married again.
Each morning, John would walk over to Nari’s apartment building and meet her in front
of the lobby. They’d walk down to the basement parking, get into her Volvo and drive to Rose
Salon. In the evening, unless John’s kids picked him up, which was rare because they were
working or at school, she’d drive them back to her building, and he’d walk home. They didn’t eat
dinner together. Each night, he’d bow, say thank you for the ride, and wish her good night.
After she parked her car, Nari would rush to her apartment, wash off her makeup and
change out of the dress-up clothes, and put on a pair of clean pajamas. In the small kitchen, she’d

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 599
fix herself a bowl of popcorn and watch two rented drama videos and go to bed early. In the
morning, she’d make herself a large breakfast of rice, fried eggs, soup, and side dishes.
Her daughter Yun worried about her living alone, but Nari couldn’t imagine living with
anyone else. Nari was still nice looking, and at church, the other women deacons who knew
about her husband leaving mentioned fixing her up with men seeking a nice, hard-working wife.
“Thank you for thinking of me, but I am still married.”
She felt no wish to take care of another man. Nari intended to age as well as possible and
live quietly. When she wrote to her three brothers that her husband Joonho was gone, none of
them had advised her to marry again. Two of them asked her to send money for their mother,
who was suffering from dementia, so of course, Nari did.
She matured. Each month, Nari put aside half of whatever was left of her pay in a
retirement savings account. On Sunday afternoons, she drove to South Coast Plaza and window
shopped. Now and then, she’d try on a one-piece dress or a skirt, but thinking of her eventual
retirement, she did her best to refrain from buying anything. It amazed her how much money
she’d spent over the years on clothing, shoes, and bags. Having her husband leave her with a
large promissory note to pay off while their daughter was in college had taught her that she
should have saved more money.
She saved also for Joonho, who she believed would eventually return, if not for her but
for their daughter. This was what happened in dramas about true love, and Nari believed that
their love had been genuine from the start. They’d had troubles, and if both of them had been
more self-controlled, they’d still be together.
Her husband was not heroic but he was a very good person. Nari thought about him often.

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 600
Joonho had made mistakes. Weak and ashamed of how life had turned out, he was trying his luck
in Brazil again. After selling the store, she’d sent him money, and on Christmas, he called her for
the first time in years. She’d been writing him now and then and knew from his cousin’s wife
that he got the letters. He knew Yun was married and she got her green card.
“How is Yun?” he asked.
“She’s happy with her husband.”
“I wanted to wish you a Merry Christmas,” he said quietly. “You’ve always liked
Christmas more than me.”
Nari laughed. In Seoul, she’d decorated their home with three trees, all their stores, and
insist on buying all their employees expensive presents.
“I better go,” Joonho said.
“Where are you working?” she asked, wanting details.
“I’m driving a truck but I found a fabric store. That money you sent was helpful. I don’t

aloe vera supplement business that had gone bust and that very day, he thought of returning to

your health.”

Lion gave his talk on the legend of Hong Gildong twice—one version for the primary and middle
school children at Exodus, and another for the high school students at Fortress. The primary
message was “Hong Gildong is a character from a fable, and he cannot serve as our role model.”
He told them none of them needed to be like Hong Gildong—a boy with supernatural
powers of intellect and wit, who tries to save the larger community and earn his station in life.
“Rather,” Lion said, “Use and nurture the talents you have. Show up and do the best you
can on whatever you put your hands to on a regular basis. Be honest and good to yourself and

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 767
others. Avoid comparisons. Each of you is needed on the team. I like you right now. Just as you
are.”
The children seemed a bit confused but relieved, too. Lion Teacher always knew their
names, said hello to everyone, and looked you in the eye when he spoke to you. They already
knew he wanted to lighten their burden.
At the version at Fortress, Jonathan Park, a senior boy from Troy High School raised his
hand during Q & A.
“My mom said that you have the highest I.Q. in California, so maybe you don’t have to
try as hard?” Jonathan said smiling, and the other children laughed.
“Wise guy,” Lion smiled back at the tall senior, “To the best of my knowledge, not the
highest I.Q. in California. You are wrong, sir, about something very important. I tried very hard
when I was your age to learn. I still try very hard now to be the head of this organization that is
only one factor of your education.” He was constantly stressing how important their regular
school teachers were, who did nearly all the difficult work five days a week.
“Everything takes an enormous amount of effort for me, but I want to give it that effort. I
don’t believe I.Q. really measures intelligence. I know for certain that I.Q. does not measure
success in life. There are many, many successful people in life who never finish high school.”
Greg Kim, a senior from Oxford, in the front row raised his hand. Lion looked at him and
nodded.
“No offense, Lion Teacher, and I ask this out of respect, but what are you not successful
at?”

After Lion gave the talks, he sat in his office and reviewed his lecture notes and thought about

#
Like yeast in dough, the Hong Gildong archetype permeated the fabric of so many important
dramas and films, and therefore the mindset and culture of nearly every striving Korean. Lion
felt compelled to warn the children of its unbearable weight. Trying to be a Korean superhero
was a terrible way to live because you might think that life has no value unless you were
exceptional at absolutely everything and able to rescue others, often at great peril to yourself.
When he first explained this to his wife, she seemed irritated that he was criticizing her
cherished dramas, which he wasn’t doing exactly. For days, he thought about the theory, and

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 770
after church on Sunday, when he spotted Bo in the patio having lunch, he broke down the theory,

If Lion had wanted to be the Hong Gildong of music, he might have lost his life’s
mission. He saw then that even thinking of wishes as something to win or lose was immature.
Having the wish, exercising any given talent, and practicing a craft should have been enough.
There would always be outside factors which he couldn’t control.
He disliked setting target goals but in his experience as a hagwon teacher, everyone
expected them, including the students. But having worked with so many students, he had learned
that it was never the goal—however reasonable or lofty—but rather, the steady execution of
habits, reliable structure and available resources, personal attitude and motivation, and
psychological makeup of the individual which factored into a person’s growth and possibilities.

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 771
Lion felt like he had tutored every kind of student, and the wider his data set, the more humbled
he felt about education.
At Exodus, he and Yun accepted as many kids as they could. Not including staff, the
building and annex had capacity for two hundred students, and as long as a child was healthy and
had decent manners, they accepted the child. They had waiting lists, but Lion refused to expand
the number of seats. The profit margins for Exodus were abysmal, and if they expanded, the
profits might grow incrementally, but he didn’t want to run a larger operation. It was never easy
to find teachers who could handle larger classrooms, and he didn’t want to raise prices. Since it
was a safe, well-run place where the kids liked going and did well enough, even the poorest of
the working parents did their best to pay on time. They were always cheaper than a sitter.
At Fortress, Peter and Mido capped enrollment to a hundred regular students, but they
could have easily had two hundred. Again, the owners and directors felt they wouldn’t have been
able to deliver the best results. Already, due to the high demand, they were able to pick the most
high performing ones, who in many cases, only needed to have their motivations realigned and
given better methods of studying. It also came down to sheer numbers for college admits. If they
had fifty students applying in a year, not all of them could get into their top choices if the top
choice was, say, Stanford.
The students at Fortress wanted to work, and often, they ended up getting the results their
parents expected. Unlike Exodus, which catered to working and middle class Korean families, in
line with the hagwons of Irvine, a wealthier community in Orange County, the fees for Fortress
were high, and the profits on Fortress subsidized Exodus, which took much more work to operate
yet made far less money.

at life. How was it possible for an eleven or thirteen year old to think he was dumb?
“I’m not as smart as my brother,” a kid would say, or “My mom says, I get bad grades

Lion didn’t blame the schoolteachers or parents. He knew from experience that everyone
wants a child to flourish but everyone had different ideas of how to make that happen. He
worried about the kids. Lion wanted them to learn better so they could feel stronger. He wanted
them to be able to solve super problems, not to be super anything.

For years, Mrs. Im, the housekeeper, had understood the relationship between Sonya and the
Chairman. More aunt than servant, Mrs. Im was devoted to her generous employer, Sonya Cho,
who had entered the Mun household as a young bride for the Chairman’s nephew and heir, Yong-
gil. As lady of the house, Sonya was nothing like the Chairman’s late wife— a capricious
daughter of a former cabinet member who could not be gracious to anyone she felt was below
her social class.
The Mun family fascinated Mrs. Im. Like vivid characters in her morning drama, she
watched Sonya; her husband, President Yong-gil Mun; his uncle, Chairman Hong-gyun Mun;

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 799
and the two boys Seungman and Jiman, whose diapers she had changed. She knew the favorite
dishes of every member of the family, their general dislikes, private interests, goals, allergies,
and of course, their formal and informal acquaintances.
From the very start, the housekeeper took to Sonya, admiring the young secretary’s fine
manners and humble demeanor despite her natural beauty and excellent education. In the ensuing
years, Sonya changed little despite the rise in her station. If anything, the more she was given,
the more she gave away.
Sonya treated everyone fairly and with great consideration, remembering birthdays,
weddings, funerals, and illnesses of those who worked for the family. To be connected to the
Chairman’s household was to be protected under Sonya’s umbrella of concern.
Mrs. Im was unable to finish high school; however, she was more capable than some of
the Chairman’s brightest employees who received MBAs from abroad. She missed nothing,
especially the wants and needs of her employers.
With so much warmth between them, the Chairman and Sonya did not appear as former
boss and secretary. By the way they considered each other’s expressions with deep, abiding
interest, they did not look like father-in-law and daughter-in-law. Lacking the casual boredom
brought by the expectation of an eternal bond, they would not be mistaken as husband and wife
either.
In the eyes of a sensitive observer, the two were undeniably lovers connected by yearning
and fear of loss. Exquisite manners and honorific language covered the public interactions
between the Chairman and Sonya like a fine silk gauze. At home, it was possible to measure the
physical space between them, which was closer than Sonya’s and her husband.

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 800
Like his uncle, Yong-gil was a stickler about language, and although he was sufficiently
fair to the household staff as well as to his employees, he could be cool and rigid, unable to
garner their affection. His business competence shielded him from criticism, and his formal tone
kept him at a distance from almost everyone except his sons.
On Friday evening, he came home to change before heading out again. At the door, Mrs.
Im greeted him and hung up his raincoat.
“Good evening, Deacon Im.”
Yong-gil removed his black cap-toe oxford dress shoes. She picked up his shoes and
returned them to the right shelf in the President’s private shoe closet, withdrew his bespoke
leather slippers from the bottom shelf. Mrs. Im knelt on the floor to place the slippers in the
appropriate direction of his stocking feet.
“Is everyone home?”
“The Chairman and Madam are here, but the young masters will not be at dinner. Madam
said you would not be dining at home—”
“That is correct. I want to shower and change. I have a work dinner.”
Mrs. Im, older than the Chairman by a few months, a church deacon of two decades, and
mother of three grown children, was not a modern person with liberal moral and romantic
sensibilities; however, she knew well what it was like to be married to a philanderer. Mrs. Im
was not fooled. The President did not have a work dinner. On Friday evenings, he went to room
salons. Over the years, Mrs. Im had met no less than half a dozen of his mistresses who had
barged into the house to hassle Sonya.

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 801
Chairman’s nephew was ungrateful and over entitled, blind to his true riches. Unlike the
uncle who preferred the poor over the wealthy, the nephew who had grown up in relative
privilege was a two-faced playboy who remembered to say please and thank you to his
employees but could fire the household driver through his corporate secretary for being a few
minutes late. Never did he dole out any punishment himself. Always, he asked his secretary, Mr.
Yi, who everyone called “The Sword,” to do the worst.
After Yong-gil was promoted to President of Mun Realty at forty-five years old,
bypassing several senior members of the company, rather than being considerate to the
executives who had helped to build the successful company, he terminated those who didn’t
praise the decision. Then, he hired his smartest friends from university, shedding anyone whose
background and attitude he deemed unsuitable for his vision of the future of Mun Realty.
Unlike the Chairman who disdained hostess bars and room salons, the President preferred
the most selective ones. To the women who worked there, the President was nice looking,
wealthy, and aloof. He wore designer clothes. Naturally they fell in love with him. In hotel
rooms, he made beautiful promises, and girlfriends came to the house to realize their dreams, and
Mrs. Im was their first point of entry.
In her office, Sonya met each young woman, served tea or coffee in fine china, and
disabused her of any illusions about her husband Yong-gil. In the large kitchen, Mrs. Im chatted
with the cook and waited to be called to show the guest out. When she cleared the tea tray, the
cook would eat the untouched biscuits and leave the chocolates for Mrs. Im.
The housekeeper was on Sonya’s side. On births, deaths, weddings, holidays, and trips,
Sonya gave each employee an envelope of cash to mark the occasion. When she went to a famed

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 802
bakery to buy treats for the family, she brought back as many for the staff. Everyone was equal.
In this way, Sonya was unlike the President and more like the Chairman, an orphan who had
built his real estate company from the earnings of well-timed real estate bets.
Years earlier, even before the boys were born, Sonya discovered Mrs. Im crying in the
pantry. When she learned that Mrs. Im’s oldest had a fight at school and had broken another
child’s arm, requiring payment of his hospital bills and a legal settlement, Sonya advanced her
the full amount without telling the Chairman’s wife and Mrs. Im’s husband, who worked as one
of the two family drivers.
Mrs. Im would never tell a soul what she knew about the Chairman and Sonya, including
her own husband, because when he drank, he talked too much. Life had been fair enough to Mrs.
Im, and except for a troublesome husband, who was not all bad, she found joy in the
accomplishments and good lives of her children, each of whom had finished college, been hired
for respectable jobs, and married nice people. She was a grandmother of three children, and each
day before work, she went to Myeong-dong Cathedral to pray for her family and the Mun
household.
As long as her husband did not bring home any diseases and didn’t get into any big
trouble, Mrs. Im didn’t care about the cheating and the drinking. None of it was very serious.
Men did foolish things, and he was too old to change. Her son and two daughters took her side
always, so if her husband left her for another woman, at least, she would have the love of her
children and money of her own. More than once, Sonya had told Mrs. Im, that if she ever needed
a place to live, she could have her pick of the rooms in the servants’ quarters.
Although Mrs. Im had been in love with her husband when she married, she had never

When Lion and Yun made the announcement about Fortress Seoul in their email newsletter, over
six hundred students applied for their pilot program for Korean students who wanted to attend
college in the United States. In the first year, they had room for fifty students. Renee and Lion
agreed that forty students would pay a reasonable, market-rate tuition, and ten students would
receive full scholarship, but no one was allowed to discuss one’s financial status and if anyone
did, the offending student would face expulsion. Since nearly all international students paid full
freight tuition, Renee and her company pledged to provide a four-year private scholarships for
the ten students.
Through assessments, Lion established a floor of high aptitude then from that pool, he
chose students by lottery. Standardize then randomize. In addition to the hagwon tuition
payments and pledge of college tuition for 10 scholarship students, Renee’s family provided
Fortress Seoul office space, dorm rooms, and airfare for the overseas tutors. Lion and Yun would
figure out the math to make the numbers work so that the pilot program wouldn’t lose money.

MJ Lee / AMERICAN HAGWON RCW LITERARY AGENCY 8.22.25 / 914

been too expensive for him to do by himself.

When Mido called her father again to check in, John didn’t answer because he’d gone to Exodus

Seated in the carpeted waiting area, Anna was reading The Silver Chair, one of the

that Danbi was away on a trip, gradually, she appeared to settle into her life in Cypress.
John didn’t know how to tell her that she might be moving to New Jersey to live with

until the school year ended.
